props.title: Stigmata
props.initialSlug: The agony, the ecstasy, the truth.

sections.content: Stigmata emerged during the late 90s supernatural thriller boom, following the success of The Sixth Sense (1999) and End of Days (1999). Patricia Arquette plays Frankie, a Pittsburgh hairdresser who mysteriously develops stigmata - the wounds of Christ - despite being an atheist. Gabriel Byrne's Father Kiernan investigates, uncovering a Vatican conspiracy involving suppressed Gospels. The film's gothic industrial aesthetic, powered by Billy Corgan's haunting score and Smashing Pumpkins tracks, creates a distinctly millennial anxiety about faith and institutional religion.

sections.content: Religious conspiracy thrillers peaked in the late 90s and early 2000s, with films like End of Days (1999) and Lost Souls (2000) combining Catholic mythology with millennium paranoia. The Ninth Gate (1999) took a similar approach, following rare book dealer Johnny Depp as he investigates demonic texts. These films reflected growing skepticism toward religious institutions while maintaining fascination with supernatural faith. SUBHEAD: Gothic Religious Horror Evolution

Stigmata distinguishes itself through its focus on a specifically Catholic phenomenon, unlike broader possession narratives like The Exorcism of Emily Rose (2005) or The Rite (2011). The film's exploration of the Gospel of Thomas and institutional corruption preceded similar themes in The Da Vinci Code (2006). Director Rupert Wainwright employs music video techniques - rapid cuts, saturated colors, industrial imagery - creating a distinctly MTV-era take on religious horror.
